Reichsbahnrat Dr.-Ing. Kühnel, Berlin: „$\textit{Die Abnutzung des Gußeisens und ihre Beziehung zum Aufbau und den mechanischen Eigenschaften.}$“
Der Verein Deutscher Eisengießereien, der Verein Deutscher Eisenbahnfachleute und der Lokomotiv-Verband haben mit dem Deutschen Reichsbahnbetrieb einen Ausschuß für die Prüfung von Gußeisen im Eisenbahnbetrieb gegründet. Der Ausschuß hatte die Aufgabe, Unterlagen für die Erkenntnis der Abnutzungsbeständigkeit des Gußeisens in der Wärme und Kälte und ihre Beziehung zu Aufbau und mechanischen Eigenschaften zu schaffen. Es wurden eine Reihe von Versuchen durchgeführt, und zwar für Bremsklötze ein Großversuch auf der Wannseebahn mit 10 Wagenzügen, die mit Bremsklötzen verschiedener Herkunft ausgerüstet waren, und Laboratoriumsversuche mit den gleichen Bremsklötzen bzw. deren Auschnitten in dem Bremsversuchsamt Grunewald und der Mechanischen Versuchsanstalt des Reichsbahnzentralamts. Für Schieberbuchsen und Ringe wurde gleichfalls ein Großversuch durchgeführt durch Ausrüstung von T-12-Lokomotiven mit Schieberbuchsen und Ringen verschiedener Härte und Lieferung und zwei Ölsorten im Lokomotiv-Versuchsamt Grunewald. Weiter wurden die Teile auf mechanische Eigenschaften, Aufbau und chemische Zusammensetzung in der Mechanischen Versuchsanstalt des Reichsbahnzentralamtes untersucht und alle aus dem Betriebe als nicht genügend abnutzungsfest beanstandeten Schieberbuchsen auf mechanische Eigenschaften und Aufbau geprüft. Zur Untersuchung der Roststäbe wurden 10 Lokomotiven mit Roststäben verschiedenen Phosphorgehalts im Vergleich mit Roststäben eines Phosphorgehalts von etwa 0.8\% ausgerüstet. Die Versuche über Bremsklötze sowie Schieberbuchsen und Ringe führten übereinstimmend zu dem Ergebnis, daß weiches ferritisches Gußeisen nicht verschleißfest ist und auch härteres Gußeisen ziemlich stark angreift. Der beste Einlauf wird erzielt bei annähernd gleicher Härte der aufeinanderlaufenden Teile und perlitischem Gefüge, jedoch muß für den besonderen Fall von Schieberbuchse und Schiebring die Buchse etwas härter sein als der Ring. Bei den Versuchen über Roststäbe wurde ermittelt, daß die Leichtflüssigkeit mancher Kohleaschen, die Schwefeleinwanderung von der Kohle her in den Roststab und die weitgehende Gefügeveränderung des Roststabes unter der Wärmeentwicklung Zerstörungsursachen sind, die die Abnutzungsbeständigkeit des Roststabes vermutlich stärker gefährden als ein hoher Schwefel- und Phosphorgehalt. Mit Rücksicht auf die mechanische Beanspruchung des Roststabes und die Bruchgefahr ist ein nicht hoher Phosphorgehalt trotzdem erwünscht.

Zivil-Ing. Mehrten, Berlin: „$\textit{Die Bedeutung der Normenbewegung für die Gießerei.}$“
Bei den steigenden Anforderungen an die Güte der Gußwaren ist der Gießereileiter gezwungen, den Neuerungen und Verbesserungen im Gießereiwesen größte Aufmerksamkeit zuzuwenden, wobei er auch die Normenbestrebung als Mittel mitwirken lassen muß, um eine Steigerung der Erzeugnisse bei stetiger Verbesserung des Betriebes zu ermöglichen. Der Vortr. erwähnte insbesondere die Erfolge der letzten Zeit in bezug auf die Herstellung hochwertigen Gußeisens. Die Vereinheitlichung bringt eine wesentliche Ersparnis an Betriebs- und Verwaltungskosten und damit auch eine Steigerung der Leistungsfähigkeit mit sich. Vortr. berichtet über die Arbeiten des Reichsausschusses für Lieferbedingungen mit dem Deutschen Normenausschuß und dem von den Gießereiverbänden eingesetzten Unterausschuß, welche ganz besonders die in der Bearbeitung kommenden Roh- und Hilfsstoffe in der Gießerei. Es sollen für Roheisen, Schmelzzusätze, Nichteisenmetalle, Legierungen, Abfallstoffe, Schrott, Altmetalle, Schmelzkoks und sonstige Brennstoffe, feuerfeste Steine, Formsande, Kohlenstaub usw., soweit sie nicht schon vorhanden, Liefernomen aufgestellt werden. Was über Gütevorschriften in Herstellung, Handel und Verbrauch dieser Stoffe gesagt wurde, gilt auch für die Vereinheitlichung der Betriebsmittel, Werkzeuge und Geräte der Gießereien. Auch diese Dinge sind Gegenstand der Verhandlungen, die ebenso für den Modellbau, für Formmaschinen und Zubehör beachtlich sind.
Die in vier Gruppen der Werkstoffe für Gießereierzeugnisse: Gußeisen, Temperguß, Stahlguß und Nichteisenmetall-

guß gegebenen Ausführungen zeigen den heutigen Stand der Arbeiten. Das Normenblatt „Gußeisen“, Klasseneinteilung und Werkstoffeigenschaften, ist als Vorstandsvorlage abgeschlossen. Das Blatt „Temperguß“ liegt ebenfalls im Entwurf vor, so daß beide Blätter demnächst zur Kritik veröffentlicht werden können. Das Blatt „Stahlguß“ ist dagegen endgültig abgeschlossen, wenn auch vielleicht später einige Ergänzungen zugefügt werden müssen. Wesentlich mehr Schwierigkeiten bieten die Liefernormen für Nichteisenmetalle und Legierungen. Diese werden im Fachnormenausschuß für Nichteisenmetalle in Verbindung mit der Deutschen Gesellschaft für Metallkunde, den in Frage kommenden Industrieverbänden, Behörden und Instituten für Metallforschung bearbeitet. —

Geh. Regierungsrat Dr. Ing. Mathesius, Berlin: „$\textit{Der Kupolofen in Theorie und Praxis der letzten Jahrzehnte.}$“ Die Schmelzleistung von Kupolöfen steht in einem gesetzmäßigen Zusammenhang mit der Windmenge, die je Minute und Quadratmeter Ofenquerschnitt durch den Ofen hindurchströmt. Die günstigsten Schmelzverhältnisse werden bei gutem Koks bei einer Satzkkokshöhe von etwa 8% erhalten, bei welcher gleichzeitig eine Stundenschmelzleistung von 10 t je Quadratmeter Ofenquerschnitt erreicht wird, wenn die Windmenge etwa 100 cbm je Minute und Quadratmeter Ofenquerschnitt beträgt. Sowohl bei Vermehrung als auch bei Verminderung dieses Windquantums werden die Resultate ungünstiger und die im Ofen erzielbaren Eisentemperaturen niedriger. Eine Vermehrung der Satzkkoksmenge gibt eine erhebliche Verminderung in der Stundenschmelzleistung und ebenfalls niedrigere Eisentemperatur. Bei einer Verminderung der Satzkkoksmenge entsteht die Gefahr einer zu niedrig liegenden Schmelzone und dadurch einer Steigerung des Abbrandes sowie einer Erschmelzung von gasreichem Eisen. Die maximale Eisentemperatur, welche ein Kupolofen unter normalen Betriebsbedingungen zu leisten vermag, liegt innerhalb der Grenzen von $1450$--$1500\,^\circ\text{C}$. Mit diesen Feststellungen scheint das Problem des Schmelzens von Eisen in Kupolöfen in allen wesentlichen Punkten geklärt zu sein. —

Dr.-Ing. W. Claus, Berlin: „$\textit{Die Beziehungen zwischen Formart und Festigkeitseigenschaften bei Metallguß und über das Normformungsverfahren.}$“
Der Vortr. berichtete über die Festigkeitseigenschaften von Gußstücken in Abhängigkeit von der angewandten Formart. Die Klärung dieser Frage ist von ganz besonderer Wichtigkeit für die Metallgießereien, da heutzutage weitgehend Bestrebungen bestehen, die teuren und zeitraubenden Handformen durch das Naßformverfahren zu ersetzen. Zu diesem Zwecke führte der Vortr. gemeinsam mit Cand.-Ing. Friedrich Goederitz eine Untersuchungsreihe an gegossenem Reinaluminium, Al-Cu-Legierung und einer Aluminium-Kupfer-Legierung aus. Als Ergebnis wird berichtet: untersucht wurde in Kokille, grüne und trockene Sandformen vergossenes Material, und die Zahlenwerte der Härte, der Zerreißfestigkeit und Dehnung und der Schlagarbeitswerte wurden ermittelt. Bei den verwendeten Gießmaterialien wurden ebenfalls untersucht. Bei der amerikanischen Legierung, also der Aluminium-Kupfer-Legierung ohne Zink, fiel die Bruchfestigkeit beim Übergang vom Kokillenguß zum Naßsandguß um etwa 50 % ab; beim Übergang vom Naßsandguß zum Trockensandguß konnte ein Abfall beobachtet werden. Beim Übergang von der Trockenform zur Naßform war eine geringere Abnahme der Festigkeitswerte zu verzeichnen als beim Übergang vom Naß- zum Trockensandguß. Im allgemeinen war der Übergang der Werte vom Trockenform- zum Naßformguß nicht so groß. Die Untersuchungen ergaben, daß die Materialeigenschaften in grünnaß gegossenen Materials im allgemeinen schlechter waren als diejenigen des in trockenem Sand gegossenen Materials. Die Materialwerte von Kokillenguß übertrafen diejenigen beider Sandgußarten bedeutend. Zusammenfassend ist zu sagen, daß in mechanisch-technischer Hinsicht dem Naßformverfahren in den Metallgießereien keine Bedenken bestehen.

Die Neubearbeitung des wichtigen Werkes steht ganz im Zeichen der seit Ausbruch des Weltkrieges gänzlich umgestalteten Produktions- und Absatz-Verhältnisse. Auf eine möglichst vollständige Wiedergabe der durch die neuen Wirtschaftsbedingungen verursachten Verschiebungen ist großer Wert gelegt. Für den Gebrauch des Buches ist es sehr zu begrüßen, daß an der Spitze der einzelnen Kapitel stets eine Zusammenstellung der einschlägigen Fachliteratur gebracht ist. Der Stoff ist wesentlich erweitert durch Aufnahme neuer Abschnitte über die Arsen-, Kobalt- und Lithiumverbindungen der Mineralwelt. Eine gedrängte Darstellung der Kali- und Magnesiasalze und ihrer wirtschaftlichen Weltbedeutung ist gleichfalls neu aufgenommen. Durch den so wesentlich vermehrten Stoff wurde der Umfang jedoch nicht allzusehr vergrößert, weil die in der ersten Auflage gegebenen Ausführungen über die chemischen Untersuchungsmethoden, welche der inzwischen verstorbene Pufahl verfaßt hatte, in der Neubearbeitung nicht mehr zum Abdruck kamen. Diese Beschränkung ist durchaus in der Annahme gerechtfertigt, daß die Literatur der chemisch-technologischen Untersuchungen speziell der natürlichen Rohstoffe in vielen ausgezeichneten Handbüchern erschöpfender behandelt ist, als es in einem Werke der vorliegenden Art möglich ist. Es ist hoch anzuerkennen, daß trotz der großen Anzahl der Mitarbeiter und der Verschiedenheit ihres speziellen wissenschaftlichen Standpunktes doch ein so durchaus einheitlich gediegenes Material geboten wird. Viele Kapitel sind gegenüber der ersten Auflage sehr vertieft worden. Das Buch wird in seiner neuen Form auch dem wissenschaftlichen Forscher wie dem Praktiker ein wertvolles und unentbehrliches Hilfsmittel sein.

Konstante der Kohle zu sein.

In addition, the basal cell surfaces of ameloblasts and the stratum intermedium cells showed an intense enzymatic reaction. Maturation Ameloblasts

The enzymatic activity of Ca- and Mg-ATPase decreased steeply from secretory to maturation stage ameloblasts. Both enzymes showed an identical distribution pattern and intensity in the maturation ameloblasts. In both ruffle-ended and smooth-ended maturation ameloblasts, the enzymatic activity was limited to the basal cell surfaces facing the papillary layer. The lateral and distal cell surfaces, including the ruffle borders, showed no enzymatic reaction (Figs. 7–10). Except for minute deposits of reaction products in the Golgi membranes, all other cell organelles showed a negative reaction (Fig. 10). A positive enzymatic reaction was also noted along the plasma membranes of papillary cells, except in gap junctions (Figs. 7 and 9).

When the tissues were incubated in the medium for Ca-ATPase lacking levamisole, an intense enzymatic activity was found in Golgi membranes and a slightly less intense reaction was noted in mitochondrial membranes and in tubular structures of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum near the ruffled borders (Figs. 11 and 12). The plasma membranes of the ruffled borders also showed a weak reaction when levamisole was not used. The basal cell surfaces of ameloblasts and the papillary cell surfaces exhibited a similar distribution and intensity pattern with or without levamisole in the incubation medium.
On the other hand, when the tissues were incubated in medium for Mg-ATPase lacking levamisole, an intense reaction appeared on the extra-

cellular aspect of the plasma membranes of the ruffled border. The basal cell surfaces of maturation ameloblast were positive while the lateral cell surfaces seldom showed any reaction (Figs. 13 and 14). Mitochondrial and Golgi membranes contained only a few deposits of reaction products. Papillary cell plasma membranes also showed a very weak enzymatic activity (Figure 13).
Negative Controls and Ca Dependency

In control sections incubated in medium lacking ATP, no reaction product was observed in the plasma membranes or in any cell organelles of both secretory and maturation ameloblasts (Fig. 15). Omission of the enzyme activator $\text{CaCl}_2$ from the medium for Ca-ATPase also provided negative evidence of enzymatic reaction in the cells of the enamel organ (Fig. 16).
Effect of Trifluoperazine on Ca-ATPase

At 2 hours after trifluoperazine administration, enzymatic reaction of Ca-ATPase disappeared almost completely from the plasma membranes of secretory ameloblasts. A weak reaction was still observed in the basolateral cell surfaces in the infranuclear region of secretory ameloblasts (Fig. 17). Trifluoperazine administration, however, did not affect Ca-ATPase activity in the cells of the stratum intermedium and the papillary layer (Fig. 17). In saline-injected rats, Ca-ATPase activity of enamel organ cells was observed in the same distribution pattern and intensity as in normal rats described above (data not shown).
Discussion

Cytochemical and biochemical demonstrations of substrate-specific ATPase (EC. 3.6.1.3) should be done with combined inhibition tests of nonspecific alkaline phosphatase (EC. 3.1.3.1), which is capable of hydrolyzing a substantial part of the ATP [20, 21]. Among several inhibitors, levamisole almost completely inhibits nonspecific alkaline phosphatase activity, whereas it does not affect the substrate-specific ATPase visualized by the histochemical lead technique [21, 24]. Thus, the enzymatic reaction demonstrated in our experiments after inhibition by 5 mM levamisole can be regarded to show the site of substrate-specific ATPase. When we omitted levamisole from the incubation media, we observed reaction product in the Golgi membranes, lysosomal bodies, the plasma membranes of maturation ameloblasts, and the growth region of newly secreted enamel matrix. These findings are generally in agreement with previous cytochemical observations of alkaline phosphatase in ameloblasts [20, 25–28]. In addition, some electron microscopic cytochemical studies of ATPase in secretory ameloblasts indicated matrix ATPase activity in the growth regions of rod and interrod enamel [29, 30]. We observed an identical reaction in the enamel matrix only when we omitted levamisole, a specific inhibitor for alkaline phosphatase, from the incubation media. Thus, we think that what has been described as ATPase in some cell organelles and the enamel matrix is due to overlapping reaction of alkaline phosphatase.

In a number of tissues, Ca-ATPase has been recognized as having a functional role in active transport of calcium ion across the plasma membranes [14–16, 20, 21, 31, 32]. In addition, the ouabain-insensitive portion of ATPase was separated from Na, K-ATPase and called Mg-ATPase [33], which was also thought to be responsible for calcium transport in red cells [34], intestinal mucosa cells [14], and kidney cortex cells [15]. Therefore, Ca-

and Mg-ATPase can be regarded as participating in the release of energy for active transport of calcium ions across the plasma membranes of the enamel organ cells. ATP is thought to be the major source of energy for this calcium pump.

Biochemically, Yoshimura and Suzuki [17] have shown Ca-ATPase activity in a microsomal fraction containing smooth-surfaced endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi membranes, and plasma membranes of the secretory stage enamel organ. Although their data did not identify definite membranous components of the microsomal fraction, our results made it clear that, at alkaline pH, substrate-specific Ca- and Mg-ATPase is bound to the plasma membranes of the enamel organ cells, especially of secretory ameloblasts. In our observations, the reaction for Ca-ATPase in secretory ameloblasts was much more intense than that for Mg-ATPase. This may indicate that ameloblast ATPase is activated by calcium but reduced by magnesium [3, 17].

By means of energy-dispersive x-ray microanalysis of intracellular calcium contents, Eisenmann, et al. [10] recently indicated an increased calcium concentration from the proximal to the distal cytoplasm of secretory ameloblast and speculated that this calcium gradient might be dependent upon enzyme activity. Materials and Methods
Tissues

Fifteen-day-old Sprague Dawley rats were anesthetized, briefly perfusion-fixed with half-strength Karnovsky's fixative [17] in Millonig's phosphate buffer [18] without dextrose, and decapitated. After decalcification in a 4% EDTA solution containing 0.2 M sucrose at pH 7.2 for 5 days, specimens were immediately processed for either light microscopy (LM) or transmission electron microscopy (TEM). LM specimens were paraffin-embedded and 5 $\mu$m serial sections were cut through the area of the developing third molars and the surrounding resorbing bone. Every tenth section was stained with hematoxylin and eosin, for both orientation and demonstration of osteoclasts. TEM specimens were trimmed, postfixed in osmium, dehydrated through a graded series of alcohols, and embedded in Spurr resin [19]. Ultrathin sections of resorbing bone were stained with uranyl acetate and lead citrate and viewed in a Philips EM-400T transmission electron microscope.
Reagents

Detection of endogenous IgG: rabbit anti-rat IgG was obtained from Sigma Chemical Co. (St. Louis, MO, USA) and biotinylated goat anti-rabbit IgG, avidin D, and biotinylated horseradish peroxidase (HRP) were purchased from Vector Laboratories, Burlingame, CA, USA (Rabbit IgG Vectastain ABC Kit).

Demonstration of FcγR-binding: rabbit IgG and Fc-deficient ${F(ab')_2}$ fragments were obtained from Jackson Immuno Research Labs. Inc. (Avondale, PA, USA) and the Vectastain Rabbit IgG Kit was used. Biotinylated rabbit anti-goat IgG, used in control incubations, was obtained from Vector Laboratories (Goat IgG Vectastain ABC Kit). Antibodies were diluted in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for Fc$\gamma$R  incubations.

Discussion

The ABC technique for immunohistochemistry is a highly sensitive method, resulting in a low back- ground staining due to the high dilutions of anti- body employed [20, 21]. In the present study, en- dogenous rat IgG was clearly evident at the inter- face between osteoclasts and bone, in the area of the clear zone and ruffled border.

Further use of the avidin-biotin-peroxidase com- plex has recently been described by Elner et al. [16] in a technique designed to detect Fc$\gamma$R in tissue sections. Not only does this method of successive incubations provide an increase in sensitivity over conventional Fc$\gamma$R detection techniques, such as EA rosette formation or utilization of FITC-IgG but, like the conventional ABC technique referred to above, it shares a greater sensitivity over indi-. rect staining with PAP complexes due to the higher

In the present study, the use of EDTA-decalcified sections further improved morphology, antibody penetration, and specificity [22]. Although it is pos. sible that the decalcification procedure is capable of reducing the antigenicity and activity of immuno- globulin binding sites, the distinct localization of the staining and the use of rigorous control incuba- tions, combined with the fact that the Fc$\gamma$R is a membrane-bound structure, favor the interpreta- tion of a selective binding of the Fc portion of IgG to Fc$\gamma$Rs capped to the osteoclast/bone interface This is further supported by the fact that previous immunohistochemical studies on mineralized tissues have successfully used fixed and EDTA-de- calcified sections to demonstrate distribution of structural proteins [22] and enzymes such as ATP- ase [23] and other enzymes [22] in osteoclasts.

THE DEVELOPMENT OF CHEMICALLY DEFINED SUBSTRATA FOR TESTING OSTEOCLASTIC FUNCTION SJ Jones，NM Maroudas，NN Ali and A Boyde

Osteoclasts have the capacity to form resorption pits in a wide range of biological and non-biological materials (SJ Jones et al.，Anat & Embryoll70，247，l984)both when isolated from bones and cultured on the surrogate substratum and in vivo following implantation of the material. It is of obvious importance to be able to define chemically the mineral resorbed so that the range of ions that will provoke the release of an effective demineralising agent by the osteoclast can be discovered. Using Addadi and Weiner's（l985，PNAS，in press）method，we have grown calcite crystals on sulphonated polystyrene dishes so that the crystals were distributed as a nearly confluent layer with an average face length of 30 microns． These had the following advantages: they could be examined throughout the culture period by optical microscopy for resorption pits produced by the osteoclasts;they were too large to be phagocytosed by the osteoclasts;the number of calcium ions mobilised by the resorption episode could be calculated via SEM photogrammetry and resorption expressed in terms of hydrogen ion equivalents secreted by the cell; and the interspersion of the sulphonated plastic dish (which has good cell adhesion properties) or "space" meant that "double-ended" resorption，where one cell was responsible for the simultaneous production of two resorption lacunae，could be identified. The production of more than one locus of resorptive activity in an osteoclast is also a feature of in vivo resorption when osteoblasts intervene between two or more sites of attachment of an osteoclast in the bone.
Work is now in progress to substitute different ions to test further the specificity of osteoclastic demineralisation.

ANALYSES OF COLLAGENASE AND COLLAGENASE INHIBITOR
SYNTHESIS BY OSTEOBLAST-LIKE TUMOR CELLS
N.C. Partridge, S.L. Teitelbaum, J.J. Jeffrey, H.G. Welgus
and A.J. Kahn

The major organic constituent of bone matrix is Type I collagen. The degradation of this protein during bone resorption requires a collagenolytic enzyme traditionally identified as a neutral collagenase of osteoclast origin. However, more recent evidence suggests that this enzyme originates from osteoblasts not osteoclasts. In keeping with this possibility, the hormonal regulation of collagenase (C‘ase) and collagenase inhibitor (CI) synthesis was studied, in vitro, in two osteogenic sarcoma cell lines (UMR 106-01 and SaOS-2) using both functional assays and ELISA determinations. UMR 106-01 produced no detectable C'ase under basal conditions, but synthesized 93 and 73 ng/$10^6$ cells, respectively, of the enzyme when treated with $10^{-7}$M parathyroid hormone (PTH) and $10^{-6}$M prostaglandin E$_2$ (PGE$_2$) for 72h. Other established bone-resorbing agents including,1,25(OH)$_2$ vitamin D, epidermal growth factor (EGF) and retinoic acid did not evoke C’ase synthesis. PTH also elicited an approximate 2x increase in CI production but the latter protein did not reach maximal levels until significantly later than C'ase (72-96 h vs. 12-24 h). In addition, the data showed the disappearance of C'ase from the culture media suggesting the presence of an enzyme or, perhaps, enzyme-inhibitor clearance mechanism. SaOS-2 cells, unlike UMR 106-01, demonstrated no C'ase on protracted incubation, but did show enhanced CI  when exposed to 12-O-tetradecanoyl phorbal 13-acetate (TPA) and EGF. Stimulation of CI by both agents was concentration-dependent, maximal 72 h after treatment and correlated with increases in CI mRNA as determined by Northern blot analysis. Collectively, these observations indicate that osteoblasts may produce C'ase and CI as well as type I collagen and, therefore, be important contributors in the resorptive and formative phases of bone remodeling.

COMPUTER SIMULATION OF OSTEOCLASTIC MOTILITY DURING RESORPTIVE EPISODES IN VITRO AL Smith，ABoyde and SJ Jones

Osteoclasts resorb bone intermittently and move across the bone surface between or during resorptive episodes. This may result in a line of separate pits, or conjoined pits forming an extended resorbed area. The resorption lacunae formed illustrate the track of the osteoclast which is determined by interactions with surrounding cells, interactions with the substratum and the intrinsic pattern of motility of the cell (SJ Jones et al, Scanning 7, 5, 1985). This paper investigates whether the latter can be characterised and simulated using a computer program to define the degree of choice.

A program was developed to vary the following parameters: the persistency factor - the maximum deviation from a straight line; the minimum and maximum angles of turning（Albrecht-Buehler, J cell Biol 80, 53, 1979)；the maximum and minimum distances travelled before a turn, and travelled by the cell per step，both expressed in cell diameters. Evidence from direct observation of resorption tracks and simulated patterns generated by the computer program suggest that the motility of osteoclasts closely resembles the persistent random walk exhibited by cultured fibroblasts （Gail and Boone, Biophys J 10, 980, 1970) or cell fragments (Enteneuer and Schliwa, Nature 310, 58,1984) rather than a pure random walk. However, abrupt directional changes do occur in osteoclastic motility as evidenced by the resorptive pattern，possibly as a result of cell-cell interactions.s Setting the persistency factor (Enteneuer and Schliwa) high to negate its effect on the model allowed the generation of good simulations of resorption patterns seen on bone and dentine. These results are of especial interest because of the unique interaction of the osteoclast with the surface it traverses.

A LOW TEMPERATURE RESIN METHOD FOR ENZYME HISTOCHEMISTRY OF ACTIVE BONE CELLS M.Thavarajah and J.A. Kanis.

There is a general lack of suitable methods for examining histochemical and immunocytochemical characteristics of bone cells $\underline{\text{in situ}}$ due to the difficulties in preserving anatomical integrity in adult bone during frozen section. We describe a method suitable for enzyme histochemistry on undecalcified bone. Undecalcified human trans-iliac biopsies were fixed in 2% paraformaldehyde in 0.1M sodium cacodylate buffer plus an equal volume of propanol, briefly dehydrated in propanol and embedded in a mixture of methacrylates (55% 2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate, 27% methyl methacrylate and 9% 2-hydroxyethylacrylate). The resin mixture polymerised at 4°C and the blocks were stored deep frozen. Thereafter, 5um sections were incubated for alkaline phosphatase at 21°C in 0.1M Tris-HCl buffer (pH9.0) containing 0.02% napthol AS B1 phosphoric acid, 1% ethylene glycol monomethyl ether and the reaction product was post-coupled with 0.08% fast blue BBN salt. The sections were washed in PBS and incubated for acid phosphatase at 21°C in 0.1M acetate buffer (pH 5.0) containing 0.02\% naphthol AS B1 phosphoric acid, 1% EGMME and post-coupled with 4% hexazotized pararosaniline hydrochloride. They were counter-stained with 1% methyl green, dehydrated and mounted. Alkaline phosphatase activity was detected as a blue reaction product on the external surface of osteoblasts overlying osteoid seams. Acid phosphatase activity was seen as a red reaction product within multinucleated osteoclasts and in some mononuclear cells in the marrow. This method allows simultaneous visualisation of alkaline and acid phosphatase activities in osteoblasts and osteoclasts respectively in undecalcified bone sections of good morphological quality.

IN VITRO DIFFERENTIATION OF OSTEOBLASTS ISOLATED FROM
MOUSE CAUDAL VERTEBRAE.
R. Lomri and P.J. Marie.

Several investigators have attempted to isolate osteoblasts from normal bone tissue using various enzymatic, mechanical or cloning procedures. However most of the culture preparations described were basedon enzymatic digestion, or pertain to multiple cell populations or to periosteal cells derived from calvaria. We have developed a simple and reliable method for isolating osteoblasts from mouse trabecular bone using a mechanical rather than enzymatic method. Caudal vertebrae （5-7） per mouse） from 10 days old mice （20-30 mice per culture) were dissected to strip off the sort tissue and the periosteal layer. The metaphyseal areas and the bone marrow were then carefully removed. The vertebrae were cut longitudinally， washed in PBS and placed on a8 80-100 µm nylon mesh. Bone explants placed on the meshes were then transferred to a plastic dish containing DMEM supplemented with 10\% fetal calf serum. After 4 days of culture， the meshes were reversed onto Primaria culture dishes and the bone cells were allowed to grow to confluence for 10 days. The cells were then recolted from the primary culture and subcultured. Phase contrast microscopic examination of the cells showed a fibroblastic appearance during the growthphase which changed into polygonal shape at confIuence. The isolated population consisted of alkaline phosphatase-positive cells with a minimal (7\%) contamination consisting of other small roundish cells. Light and electron microscopic observation of the osteoblastic cells revealed a morphological and ultrastructural appearance of typical osteoblasts. Osteoblasts grown in the presence of 10 mM β-glycerophosphate. and 50 µg/ml of ascorbic acid intercellular substance identified as collagen fibrils by histochemical procedure and EM observation. Numerous Von Kossa and Alizarin Red S stainable mineral deposits which were EDTA-removable were observed closely associated with the collagen matrix. The osteoblasts also showed an initial positive cAMP response to PTH. This method allowed us to isolate from trabecular bone.a cell population that differentiate into osteoblasts in vitro and that retain its capacity to form calcified bone tissue in culture. Using this model, numerous studies are progress to investigate the hormonal regulation of the differentiationof these endosteal osteoblastic bone forming cells.

ULTRASTRUCTURE OF THE GIANT CELL INFILTRATE OF SUBCUTANEOUSLY IMPLANTED BONE PARTICLES IN MICE S.C.Marks，Jr.，S.N. Popoff and J.L. McGuire

The giant cells of soft tissues and those of mineralized tissues (osteoclasts) have distinctly different cell surface receptors and ultrastructural characteristics. These features of giant cells on surfaces of dead, mineralized bone particles are not as well known.We have compared the cytology and ultrastructure of giant cells recruited to subcutaneously implanted isogeneic bone particles with similar features of osteoclasts in metaphyseal bone of young normal mice. Giant cells on surfaces of bone particles 2 weeks after implantation were multinucleated, had a homogeneous cytoplasm with few vacuoles and a bone surface interface unremarkable by light microscopy. In a few cells randomly distributed, small cytoplasmic vacuoles were present and large vacuoles were noted next to the bone surface at high magnification. By transmission EM extensive membrane interdigitations were prominent features on most surfaces of giant cells. In instances where these interdigitations abutted bone surfaces, configurations resembling a ruffled border were noted but these regions were always part of two different cells when examined at lower magnification or in serial sections. Breakdown of bone particles appeared to be by phagocytosis of small pieces and subsequent intracellualr digestion in electron-dense cytoplasmic vacuoles. Osteoclasts from these same young animals were smaller with fewer nuclei，had cytoplasmic vacuoles concentrated next to bone surfaces and characteristic ruffled borders and clear zones upon serial sectioning. These results confirm those of Holtrop $\underline{\text{et al}}$. (l982) that native osteoclasts and multinucleated giant cells on dead bone particles are distinctly different with respect to both ultrastructure and mechanism of disruption of bone surfaces.

DOES THE BONE-LINING CELL IN THE ADULT SKELETON HAVE OSTEOGENIC POTENTTAL?
S.C. Miller, B.M. Bowman, W.S.S. Jee

Bone-lining cells (BLC) cover inactive endosteal surfaces in the adult skeleton and may function in mineral homeostasis, although the proliferative and differentiation potential of this cell is not known. BLCs are extended along bone surfaces, have flat nuclei and the cytoplasm is often less than 0.l um thick. In adult male birds, an osteogenic response on endosteal surfaces is rapidly initiated following estrogen treatment (Dev.Biol. 87:52, 1981)．The subsequent were assessed using electron microscope autoradiography. In control,untreated birds, the density of cells adjacent to bone was about 24 cells/mm perimeter and 3H-Thymimdine (3H-TdR) labeling of BLCs was not observed. within 20 hours after estrogen treatment the labeling index (LI) had increased only modestly. Labeled BLCs were occasionally observed. The peak LI of cells apposed to bone was observed at 30 hours after estrogen treatment. At this time the surface was lined with differentiating osteogenic cells. The results suggest that the BLC in the adult skeleton retains some proliferative capacity and can be induced into the osteogenic pathway. However，the LI of the BLCs after estrogen administration cannot account for the rapid increase in osteogenic cell density on the bone surface. Thus, another source of cells, in addition to the BLC, may have contributed to the osteogenic response to estrogen in this species.

To elucidate the （haemopoietic) origin and differentiation line of the osteoclast，monoclonal antibodies against cell surface antigens on quail osteoclasts were generated. Five different tissues of the quail. None of them recognize antigens present on osteoblasts, osteocytes, fibroblasts, lymphocytes and erythrocytes.

Monoclonals OC 5.3 and OC 6.8 react with a cell surface antigen present on osteoclasts, monocytes, granulocytes and endothelium cells in liver ( sinusoidal endothelium) and in bloodvessels generally. Monoclonals OC 6.1 and OC 6.3 are highly specific for osteoclasts, but interact also with tissue macrophages in liver ( Kupffer cells ), small
intestine and lung. Monoclonal OC 6.9 interacts also in liver with bile capillairs and specific, but not identified parts of the nephron.
Our provisional conclusions are:
-The interaction of monoclonals 0C 5.3 and OC 6.8 with osteoclasts，granulocytes and monocytes corroborate to some extent the arguments for a myeloid origin of the osteoclast.

-The interaction of monoclonals OC 6.1 and OC 6.3 with osteoclasts，Kupffer cells and macrophages in smal1 intestine and lung suggest a common origin for the osteoclast and a number of well described tissue macrophages.
-The antigen 6.9 represents a functional group directly involved in an active process，in bone related to bone resorption.

hormonal regulation, the study of the separate
differentiation stages of osteoblasts and osteoclasts is crucial. We, therefore, started the production of monoclonal antibodies against cell surface antigens, specific for the various differentiation stages of the osteoclastic and osteoblastic cell lines. Here, the generation of a monoclonal antibody, highly specific for the cell surface of the osteocyte is reported.
Six day-old cultures of osteoblastlike cells (OB)
isolated from calvaria of 18 day-old chicken embryos were used to immunize mice. One of the monoclonal antibodies that were finally obtained, appeared to interact only with osteocytes. The monoclonal, OB 7.3, was tested on frozen sections of bone, liver, intestine, bloodvessel, skin and kidney. No other cell, including the mature osteoblast, was stained by OB 7.3 but the osteocyte. OB 7.3 cross reacted with osteocytes of the quail but not of the rat. OB 7.3 positive cells were present in isolated OB populations. In culture they formed a lace like network of interconnecting cell processes, very similar to the network between osteocytes in bone. OB 7.3 will enable us in the future to isolated and purify populations of osteocytes.

DIFFERENTIATION OF SKELETAL CELL POPULATIONS： M.Owen and B.Ashton

Two main methods have been used for assay of the potential for differentiation of skeletal cell populations. $\underline{\text{In vivo}}$ transplantation in an open system (subcutaneous, intramuscular, under the renal capsule) and in a closed system (diffusion chambers).Cell populations investigated are from two main sources: marrow tissue of growing or young adult long bones and soft connective tissue from the surfaces of embryonic or neonatal bones. This poster is a mini-review of the results in the literature.

In an open system, transplanted marrow cells are able to generate all the stromal cell lines (fibroblastic-reticular, adipocytic and osteogenic) and provide the tissue microenvironment necessary for establishment of marrow hemopoiesis. Fibroblastic cells obtained when marrow cells are cultured $\underline{\text{In vitro}}$ retain their osteogenic capacity. In contrast, Ob-like cell populations from embryonic and neonatal bones generate a restricted number of tissues, bone only apparently being formed with $\underline{\text{no}}$  marrow hemopoiesis. Ob-like cell populations when cultured $\underline{\text{In vitro}}$ rapidly lose their ability to form an osteogenic tissue.
Observations on similar populations assayed in diffusion chambers are in general agreement with the above.

The results could be interpreted on the following hypo- thesis. Marrow cell populations generate all known cell lines of the stromal system and are likely therefore to contain early pluripotential stem cell progenitors. The Ob-like cell populations isolated from the surfaces of fetal and neonatal bones have more restricted lineage potential and may therefore be relatively enriched in the later progenitors of the stromal system.

Receptors for 1,25-(OH)$_2$D$_3$ have been found in OB-like cells of several species.We looked at the binding characteristics and the metabolism of the ligand in the intact fetal rat OB-like (I) and rat osteosarcoma (UMR 106) OB-like cells (II).Maximal saturable binding was observed in I and II at 4 h and 2.5 h,respectively. IN VITRO STUDIES OF STROMAL STEM CELLS M.Owen and J.Cavé

According to current hypothesis stromal stem cells,
which are components of the connective tissue of bone
and marrow, give rise to a number of cell lines
including osteogenic, fibroblastic-reticular and
adipocytic lines. Fibroblastic colonies, each of
which is derived from a single stem cell (CFU-F), are
formed when suspensions of marrow cells are cultured
$\underline{\text{In vitro}}$. The colonies vary in size, morphology and expression of enzyme activity due to their origin from cells with a range of lineage potentials. Our preliminary experiments have shown that in cultures of rabbit marrow cells clonal expression of alkaline phosphatase activity, which is assumed to be a pheno typic marker for osteogenesis, is modulated $\underline{\text{In vitro}}$ by the presence in the medium of growth factors and other agents. The proportion and staining intensity of colonies expressing alkaline phosphatase activity is increased by the presence of hydrocortisone and reduced by epidermal growth factor. Clonal analysis using phenotypic markers is being developed as an assay for stromal stem cell differentiation. Such an assay would provide a tool for identifying factors which regulate the committment of stromal stem cells to osteogenic or other lines of the stromal system.

DIRECT AND INDIRECT RADIATION EFFECTS ON OSTEOCLAST FORMATION FROM PERIOSTEAL PROGENITORS IN VITRO B.A.A. Scheven, E.W.M. Kawilarang-de Haas, A.M. Wassenaar and P.J. Nijweide

Periostea of 18-day-old embryonic mouse calvaria were isolated and co-cultured with stripped 17-day-old metatarsal bones. Osteoclasts (OC's), derived from proliferating progenitors in the periostea, first resorbed the bone collar and subsequently the calcified cartilage matrix. Irradiation of the periostea prior to co-cultured led to a dose dependent decrease in OC formation. At a dose of 2.5 Gy about 85\% inhibition occurred, while at higher doses (5.0-10.0 Gy) OC formation was completely inhibited. Analysis of the obtained radiation survival curve yielded a $D_0$ value (i.e. dose required to reduce "survival" to 37 per cent of control) of about 2.5 Gy. When the bones, instead of the periostea, were subjected to irradiation before co-culture, OC differentiation was not significantly affected in the low dose range (1.0-5.0 Gy). Administration of high radiation doses (7.5-10.0 Gy), however, caused severe inhibition of OC formation. Moreover, the OC's formed in the irradiated bones appeared to be inhibited in their resorption activity. The results demonstrate that radiation primarily affects OC formation via direct action on radiosensitive, proliferating progenitors at relatively low doses. The $D_0$ value of periosteal osteoclast progenitors, obtained in the co-culture system used, corresponds well with $D_0$ values of hemopoietic progenitors using in vivo/in vitro colony forming assays. At high radiation doses (often employed locally in radiotherapy) injury to bone and cartilage may also lead to severe disturbance of bone dynamics. The indirect radiation effect may be ascribed to inhibition of production and/or release of factors promoting proliferation and differentiation of OC progenitors and OC activity.

OSTEOCLAST GENERATION FROM DIFFERENT BONE MARROW FRACTIONS AND ISOLATED HEMOPOIETIC STEM CELLS IN VITRO

Hemopoietic stem cells were isolated according to the
three-step method of Visser et al. (J.Exp.Med. 59:1576, 1984). Bone marrow cells from adult mice were fractionated by equilibrium density centrifugation on a discontinuous metrizamide gradient and simultaneously labelled with WGA-FITC. Then the WGA-positive cells were sorted by FACS. Finally, the sorted cells were further fractionated on the
ground of H-2K binding yielding a highly enriched hemopoietic stem cell population. At each subsequent step of the fractionation procedure the osteoclast (OC) forming potential of the cell population was tested in a co-culture system with stripped, OC progenitor-free metatarsal bones. Both low density and high density bone marrow fractions were able to form OC's during co-culture. However, the on-
set of OC formation from the high density cells took generally place at an earlier time point, whereas the low density cells yielded more OC's using critical cell doses. WGA sorting divided the low density cell population in an OC forming ($(WGA^+)$) and a non-OC forming ($(WGA^-)$) fraction. H-2K sorting further increased the OC forming potential of the isolated fraction. However, addition of a stem cell activating factor was needed to activate the predominantly
quiescent stem cells in this fraction. The results indi-
cate that the low density fraction contains a more immature OC progenitor subpopulation with a greater proliferation capacity than the high density OC subpopulation. Further enrichment of hemopoietic progenitor and stem cells by sorting of low density cells for high WGA and H-2K binding yields cell population with an higher OC forming capability. In conclusion, direct evidence has been obtained for the hemopoietic descendance of the OC. The question along which particular hemopoietic lineage OC progenitors differentiate has, however, yet to be elucidated.

Fluorine Concentration Changes in Human Periodontally Diseased Tooth Roots Following Several Treatment Times with Citric Acid
W. J. Sampson$^1$ and A. W. Crawford$^2$
$^1$Department of Dentistry, The University of Adelaide, Adelaide, South Australia; and $^2$School of Physics, Flinders University, Adelaide, South Australia

$\textbf{Summary.}$ Citric acid conditioning of exposed cementum has become an important adjunct to the clinical management of periodontal disease, and aggressive root planing is recommended to remove hypermineralized and endotoxin-laden diseased cementum. A nuclear resonance reaction technique was used to examine fluorine concentration changes subsequent to application of citric acid (pH 1.0) to the periodontal disease-exposed cementum surfaces of human tooth roots. The technique does not require the test teeth to be sectioned, thereby permitting longitudinal assessments of changes in fluorine concentration and minimizing measurement errors due to the considerable biological variation found between individuals. Initial fluorine concentrations ranged from 0.9%-2.4%, and maxima occurred within 4-6 μm of the surface, suggesting the presence of a hypermineralized layer. Within 60 sec, the citric acid had effectively removed the hypermineralized layer and the previously observed fluctuations in fluorine concentration leveled out at 0.3%-0.5%. Although the results indicated rapid removal of the hypermineralized layer and establishment of fluorine levels normally found in healthy cementum, the experimental design did not permit appraisal of potential effects upon the organic components of periodontally-exposed cementum.
$\textbf{Key words:}$Fluorine — Periodontal disease — Citric acid.
The use of acid demineralization as an adjunct to the clinical treatment of periodontally diseased

tooth roots was first reported by Younger in 1897
and Stewart in 1899 [1]. Register [2] has rekindled
intense interest in the prospect of encouraging new
cementum and fibrous attachment and Register and
Burdick [3] recommend that citric acid (pH. 1.0)
conditioning for 2–3 min provides optimal potential
for reattachment. Subsequently, there has been
considerable debate whether citric acid enhances
clinically significant reattachment [4–13] or has
minimal influence on the healing process [14–18].
Root planing is generally recommended to (a) re-
move ``porous'' or ``infected'' cementum, (b) re-
move ``foreign body'' cementum, (c) eliminate cal-
culus, (d) remove ``softened'' cementum, (e) pre-
pare a smooth surface to facilitate plaque control,
(f) inhibit further plaque accumulation, and (g) re-
move hypermineralized cementum [19]. It is be-
lieved the hypermineralized cementum might pre-
vent citric acid demineralization and consequent
exposure of collagen fibers thought to be necessary
in successful reattachment [20, 21].

Although it is not always possible to clinically determine when, or if, the cementum layer has been removed, vigorous root planing is usually advocated to offer the best chance of removing cementum-bound endotoxin. However, this may be at the expense of creating root hypersensitivity [22]. According to Crigger et al. [4], citric acid treatment has no effect upon nonroot-planed, periodontally-diseased root surfaces. In addition, failure to adequately root plane apparently reduces the effectiveness of other chemical preparation techniques; for example, 15% EDTA, sodium hypochlorite, 2% sodium deoxycholate, and 5% Cohn's plasma fraction IV [21]. Moreover, only root-planed surfaces permit significant attachment and growth of fibroblasts in culture, regardless of whether or not citric acid is used [18], but the number of attached cells reportedly increases with fibronectin and citric acid pre-

acid treatment times upon nonroot-planed ce-
mentum surfaces exposed to the oral cavity by
chronic periodontal disease. Of particular interest
was the possible inhibitory effect of the hypermin-
eralized layer upon citric acid conditioning and the
often stated need to root plane in order to remove
the hypermineralization.
Materials and Methods

Human teeth, extracted because of long-standing periodontal disease, were collected and rendered anorganic in 5% sodium hypochlorite for 22 h. Thereafter, the teeth were thoroughly washed and stored in distilled water prior to examination. All
teeth displayed extensive exposed cementum, had no discern-
able root caries or erosion, had not received any form of peri-odontal therapy, and came from middle-aged Caucasian patients with similar fluoride intake, ignorant of oral hygiene and lacking a desire to keep their teeth.
Fluorine Depth Profiles

Nuclear resonance reaction profiles were recorded in the Pelletron Accelerator, School of Physics, Melbourne University, according to the procedure reported by Crawford et al. [24]. The resonance reaction used was $^{19}\text{F}(\text{p}, \alpha\gamma)^{16}\text{O}$. The number of char-
acteristic 6–7 MeV gamma rays (γ) emitted via this reaction per number of incident protons (p), is directly related to the amount of fluorine in the irradiated area. The ratio of gamma rays to protons is referred to as the reaction yield and in a resonance reaction is highly dependent upon the proton energy. In addition,
the higher the proton energy, the further the known depth of penetration. This interdependence can be used to obtain a profile of fluorine concentration versus depth by measuring the yield of 6–7 MeV gamma rays while increasing the incident proton en-
ergy in small steps.

The fluorine concentration profile is quantified by comparing the yield-depth curves of the sample with the equivalent curves from a fluorine ($\text{CaF}_2$) standard. This technique has a relatively shallow analysis range but is effectively nondestructive.

Initial exposed cementum recordings were made on six teeth before citric acid conditioning (pH 1.0). Then the test areas were defined by nail polish and the acid was applied with cotton pellets for 30 sec. After thorough rinsing with distilled water, the

specimens were dehydrated and the second profile run was made. After testing, the same area was again treated with citric acid for 30 sec, rinsed, dehydrated, and subjected to further fluorine profiling. Therefore, comparative changes in fluorine concentration were obtained after 0, 30 and 60 sec exposure to citric acid.
The teeth were not scaled or root planed and care was taken to avoid visible calculus deposits.

The major advantages of the depth profiling technique are: (1) reproducible measurements are made to 20 μm without sectioning the teeth (assuming cementum comprises 46% inorganic hydroxyapatite with density$\text{g} \cdot \text{cm}^{-3}$) [24]; (2) sequential measurements can be made in exactly the same spot, thereby reducing intra-tooth variation; (3) the fluorine concentrations do not rely upon assumptoms concerning the Ca and P percent
weight and density of the sample.
Results
Initial Fluorine Concentrations

The intra-specimen fluorine concentration changes
with depth are presented in Figs. 1–6. With one
exception, maximum fluorine concentrations were
found at the surface, but in all samples the max-
imum occurred within the first 6 μm. Considerable
variation was observed between samples with
maxima ranging from 0.9%–2.4% fluorine. In 5 of
the 6 samples the fluorine concentration ap-
proached 0.6% at 20 μm subsurface. The exception
approached 1.2%, having peaked at 2.4% fluorine
at 5 μm subsurface.
Fluorine Concentrations After 30 Sec Citric Acid

Following 30 sec exposure to citric acid, the fluorine concentration profiles changed considerably. Specimen 1 maintained a similar pattern, beginning at 0.9% and oscillating around 0.6% fluorine over the test depth. The remaining specimens ranged from 0.2%–0.8% within the first 1 $μ$m and tended to approach a mean value of approximately 0.6%. However, the profiles varied for each individual with all specimens displaying peaks in concentration at differing depths. With the possible exceptions of specimens 1 and 2, the fluorine concentrations were generally consistently lower than precitric acid levels.
Fluorine Concentrations after 60 Sec Citric Acid

All specimens showed reduced fluorine concentra-
tions compared with the untreated and 30 sec
stages. Each individual recorded less variation and
smaller peaks in fluorine concentration with in-

creasing depth. Values that ranged from 0.3%–0.5%
at the surface remained much the same throughout
the test depth.

Figures 1 to 6 illustrate the inter- and intra-spec-
imen variations in fluorine concentrations, ex-
pressed as a function of depth. It is important to
note that the original surface would most likely have
been significantly modified with subsequent citric
acid applications. Therefore, the graph origins are
expected to have shifted to unknown, and probably
variable, extents, such that the 30 and 60 sec pro-
files cannot be accurately superimposed.
Discussion

The considerable variation in cementum fluorine concentrations reinforced the existence of normal biological differences among individuals. Moreover, the often reported existence of a $4$--$6$ μm hypermineralized surface zone [25, 26] was substantiated by the finding of greatest fluorine concentration within the first $6$ $\mu$m of all teeth tested. However, the fluorine profiles through the first $20$ $\mu$m of the untreated teeth indicated a series of fluctuating peaks which again varied among individuals. Similar variability has been observed in previous studies of fluorine distribution in enamel [27, 28].

Although the teeth tested had not been treated
with topical fluoride, the surface fluoride values
(0.9% – 2.4%) closely compared with 4 min appli-
cations of $\text{TiF}_4$ (0.7% – 2.8%) and (APF) acidulated phosphate-fluoride (1.8% – 2.6%) reported by Halset al. [29]. Beneath the surface maximum a consistent minimum fluorine concentration was apparentcirca 10 μm. This may reflect a persistent zone of demineralization produced during the initial exposure of the cementum surface and which reportedly becomes hypermineralized with time [30, 31].

The small sample size was dictated by the com-
plexity and time-consuming nature of the nuclear
resonance technique. This potential disadvantage
was offset by a number of important advantages
inherent in the technique. First, each depth profile
was derived from an area of 1 sq. mm, thus reducing
the influence of micro-variations between different
areas of the same tooth. Next, the fluorine concen-
trations were not calculated as an average value
from an assumed, density dependent volume har-
vested by chemical techniques [32]. Finally, each
fluorine profile was a repeatable signature for each
tooth and permitted the very useful advantage of
$\textit{longitudinal }$ experimentation by eliminating the need to section the teeth. Consequently, large num-
bers of teeth were not mandatory as successive
changes could be measured for the same tooth.

The 30 and 60 sec exposures to citric acid suggested that much of the surface hypermineralization disappeared in the first 30 sec. It is possible some fluorine may have been leached by the acid but it is more probable that most labile fluoride would have been lost during the hypochlorite and storage in distilled water stages. The most likely effect of the citric acid is that of hydrogen ion demineralization and calcium chelation of the fluoride-substituted hydroxyapatite. Most studies report the demineralizing effects of citric acid upon dentine which has been bared by extensive root planing procedures aiming to totally remove the cementum [1]. Nalbandian and Frank [33] believe citric acid conditioning speeds up the natural demineralization process and produces a $1$ $\mu$m electron-lucent zone, which also involves the peritubular dentine. Tveit and Selvig [34] have observed complete citric acid demineralization of the outer $3$--$5$ $\mu$m of dentine blocks (range $0$--$32$ μm) after 3 min and partial demineralization ranging from $7$--$71$ $\mu$m. The present study did not study the effects of citric acid upon dentine, but agreed with previous reports regarding variability in the etching effect. However, the depth and degree to which the exposed cementum surfaces were demineralized were not quantified because the specimens were not sectioned, and suitably reliable surface depth and density change techniques were unavailable.

Crigger et al. [4] believe topically applied citric
acid has no effect upon the hypermineralized ex-
posed cementum surface and subsequently recom-
mend root planing to remove the cementum and
reveal dentine. By contrast, the present study in-
dicated loss of the hypermineralized zone within 60
sec and might suggest a deemphasis upon the need
to vigorously root plane. However, the present
study used anorganic specimens and cannot com-
ment upon the effect of the organic matrix of the
cementum or endotoxin retention upon the clinical
action of citric acid conditioning. Despite the limi-
tations of the present study, less than 60 sec appli-
cation of citric acid resulted in the return to fluorine
concentrations comparable with levels previously
reported in normal, nonperiodontally exposed ce-
mentum [24].

The Effect of Hydroxyapatite Crystallinity on Hemolysis
John Wiessner, Gretchen Mandel, Paul Halverson, and Neil Mandel
Clement J. Zablocki Veterans Administration Medical Center, The Medical College of Wisconsin, Milwaukee, Wisconsin, USA

$\section*{Summary.}$. Crystalline hydroxyapatite is a compo nent of bone, teeth, and numerous pathological calcifications. The apatite crystal structure can accommodate a wide variety of atomic substitutions which gives apatite crystals an unusually high degree of variability in biochemical and physical properties. Apatite crystallites interact with numerous cellular systems $\textit{in vivo}$, and some of these interactions may lead to altered cellular function. One measure of crystal-membrane interactions is crystal-induced membranolysis of human red blood cells. Hemolytic potentials at constant crystal surface areas were measured at 1, 2, and 4 hours for 29 different preparations of apatite. Each apatite sample was characterized by its morphology, particle size, \% $\text{CO}_3$, zeta potential, and broadening of the (211), (112), (300), (202), and (002) diffraction maxima. Only the surface area/g and the X-ray powder diffraction line broadening showed a significant inverse correlation with hemolytic potential These parameters were related to each other, and are indications of the degree of crystallinity.
$\textbf{Key Words:}$: Hydroxyapatite — Crystal-induced hemolysis — Crystallinity.

Crystalline hydroxyapatite $\mathrm{Ca_5(PO_4)_3OH}$ has received much attention as the major component of the hard tissues of the body. The apatite crystal structure [1] can accommodate a wide variety of atomic substitutions which gives apatite crystals an unusually high degree of variability in biochemical and physical properties. In addition to its physio-

logical presence $\textit{in vivo}$, it is observed pathologically as well. Apatite is present in approximately 40\% of all kidney stones [2-5], is also associated with the arthropathy Milwaukee Shoulder syndrome [6-8], and is found in numerous other soft tissue calcifications [9]. The interaction between apatite crystals and biological membranes is involved in numerous aspects of both normal and pathological apatite deposition. Therefore, the study of apatite-membrane interaction is of considerable interest.

A factor that may be important in the growth of renal calculi is the retention of microcrystallites particularly apatite, in the urinary tract. The fixed particle theory [10] suggests that supersaturation due to a variety of causes, results in the precipitation of microcrystals which then bind to kidney epithelial membranes, allowing the microcrystals to grow and mature into stones. Specifically, microcrystallites nucleate within the tubular lumina or beneath the surface of the papillae, forming Randall's plaques [11]. These particles remain fixed and serve as nuclei for continued growth. The fixed particle mechanism explains the clinical observation of apatite-containing papillary casts [12]. Given urinary flow rates, anatomical dimensions, and states of urinary supersaturation, it is extremely unlikely that kidney stones, but not bladder stones, form without sites of fixation [10]. Whether the apatite crystals bind to the kidney membrane after they are formed, or are formed on the membrane itself, is not known at this time, but it is apparent that some kind of crystal-cell interaction does occur during the formation of kidney stones [13].

Milwaukee Shoulder syndrome is characterized by the concurrence of microspheroids of apatite crystals, active collagenase, and neutral protease in the joint fluids of patients with rotator cuff defects [6-8]. Apatite has been shown to release collagenase, neutral protease, and prostaglandins from

The (002) had a distinctly sharper profile, and the correlation between its 4 hour lysis and its domain size is shown in Fig. 6. Discussion

Previous studies on crystal-induced hemolysis have shown that atomic structure is one of the factors affecting membranolysis [18, 23, 24]; another factor is crystal morphology. Changes in morphology in-duced by grinding have been shown to affect the hemolytic potential of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate [26] and calcium oxalate monohydrate [24]. However, grinding of calcium oxalate dihydrate did not appear to influence its hemolytic potential [24]. The current study on apatites extends our knowl-edge on the structural and physical characteristics that mediate crystal-induced membranolysis. The apatites studied varied only slightly in chemical composition. These chemical substitutions could not be correlated with crystal-induced membrano-lysis.

In apatite-induced membranolysis, changes in crystal growth morphology, particle size, $\mathrm{Ca:P}$ ratio, $\%$ $\mathrm{CO_3}$, $\%$ and type of atomic substitution, and zeta potential had no apparent effect on hemo-lytic potential. These observations may be ex-plained in part by the forgiving nature of the apatite structure which tolerates minor perturbations in its crystal structure. The fact that differences in

Both the surface area/g and the X-ray powder diffraction line broadening showed a significant correlation with hemolytic potential. These param-eters are related to each other, and are indications of the quality of the crystals, i.e., the degree of crystallinity. A crystal can be thought to consist of a series of blocks in a three-dimensional array, with each block containing a basic structural repeat. As a crystal grows, the blocks can shift into slightly different orientations by as much as $0.2$--$0.5^\circ$, creating a second series of slightly misaligned crystal blocks, or domains [27]. The array of do-mains is referred to as the basic mosaic character of

the crystal. A good quality crystal would be com-posed of only a few large blocks containing many structural repeats and would have a large domain size. In comparison, a poorly crystallized sample would have a small domain size and many small misaligned blocks containing fewer structural re-peats.

Hydroxyapatite (Fig. 9) is an anisotropic struc-ture with hexagonal symmetry [1]. The preferential growth direction is along the six-fold screw sym-metry axis that defines the basic calcium-oxygen coordination geometry. The six-fold rotation axis is the crystallographic $z$-axis and is related to the (002) diffraction maxima. The hydroxyl channel is structurally disordered and runs throughout the lat-tice parallel to the $z$-axis. The diffraction maxima

Of the above keratinocytes, $4 \times 10^7$ were resuspended in 5 ml 30% Percoll (Pharmacia AB, Uppsala—colloidal suspension of silica particles coated with polyvinylpyrrolidone). A stock solution of Percoll was prepared by mixing 9 parts of Percoll with 1 part of PBS. This stock solution was then diluted by adding PBS to obtain mixtures of the desired density. The suspension in 5 ml 30\% Percoll was placed on top of a performed discontinuous Percoll gradient, consisting of 70% (8 ml), 60% (12 ml), and 14% (12 ml).

Centrifugation ($1{,}000 \times g$) for 25 min at room temperature in a fixed angle rotor yielded four different fractions of cells collected at different densities of Percoll. The cell containing regions were removed with a pipette, diluted with a fivefold amount of PBS, and centrifuged at $80 \times g$ for 10 min. The cells were washed 5 times with PBS and frozen at $-70^\circ$C for further workup. Percoll band III, which consists predominantly (more than 90%) of basal cells, and Percoll band II, comprising spinous and granular cells, as characterized by morphological, immunological, and biochemical criteria [16] were separately analyzed for calcitriol binding.
Sucrose Density Gradient Analysis

Linear 5--20\% sucrose density gradients in KTED buffer (4 ml) were prepared by using a self-designed gradient former. Samples (cytosol: 0.2 ml/1.2 mg protein; nuclear extract 0.2 ml/0.3 mg protein) were carefully layered on top of the gradients, which had been pre-equilibrated for 2 h at $4^\circ$C. The samples were centrifuged through the linear sucrose gradient at $255{,}000 \times g$ for 21 h at $4^\circ$C in a SW-60 rotor (Beckman Instr. Co.), and 7-drop fractions were collected. The sedimentation rate (in Svedberg units, S) for proteins was calculated using [$^{14}$C]labeled bovine serum albumin (4.4 S), ovalbumin (3.7 S), or $\gamma$-globulin (7.3 S) as standards.
Hydroxylapatite Assay
Receptor-bound tritiated and non-labeled vitamin D

metabolites were assayed in the cytosol fractions with the hydroxylapatite assay [17]. Aliquots, 0.5 ml, of 50% (w/v) hydroxylapatite-KTED-buffer-slurry at $4^\circ$C were added to the sample for a 15-min incubation period with frequent vortexing. The samples were then centrifuged at $12{,}000 \times g$ for 5 min. The hydroxylapatite pellets were washed three times with 2 ml buffer TED 0.5\% Triton X-100 (pH 7.4). The final washed pellet was extracted with ethanol to recover tritiated steroids. The dried extracts were dissolved in counting solution (Aquasol NEN Co.) and determined by liquid scintillation counting.
Saturation Analysis

Scatchard analysis [18] was carried out to define $K_\text{D}$ (equilibrium dissociation constant) and $N_\text{max}$ (number of binding sites). Aliquots of diluted cytosol (0.1 ml/0.6 mg protein) or nuclear extract (0.1 ml/0.3 mg protein) were incubated with varying concentrations (0.1--10 nM) of [$^3$H]1,25($\text{OH}$)$_2$$\text{D}_3$ in the absence (total binding) or presence (non-specific binding) of a 100-fold molar excess of unlabeled 1,25($\text{OH}$)$_2$$\text{D}_3$ for 16 h at $4^\circ$C. Bound [$^3$H]1,25($\text{OH}$)$_2$$\text{D}_3$ was determined using hydroxylapatite assay.
Binding of Epidermal $1,25(OH)_{2}D_{3}$ Receptors to DNA-Cellulose

DNA-cellulose (0.3 mg DNA/ml) was prepared according to the method of Alberts and Herrick [10] using highly polymerized calf thymus DNA (Type I, Sigma) and Whatman CF-11 cellulose. Each column was equilibrated in TED for 16 h at $4^\circ$C prior to use, and run at a flow rate of $5$ ml/h/cm$^2$. Samples were loaded into the columns, washed with 3-column volumes of TED, and eluted in 10 volumes with a linear gradient from 0.1 M to 0.6 M KCl in TED. Nuclear extracts (0.6 ml/1.2 mg protein) of neonatal epidermis were incubated for 2 h at $4^\circ$C with [$^3$H]1,25($\text{OH}$)$_2$$\text{D}_3$ prior to chromatography on DNA-cellulose.

Results
Competitive Receptor Studies in the Cytosol and Nucleus (Chromatin) of the Neonatal Mouse Epidermis

When cytosolic or nuclear fractions of neonatal mouse epidermis were incubated with [$^3$H]-$1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ and subsequently fractionated by sucrose density gradient centrifugation, a peak of radioactivity was found in the 3.5 S region (Fig. 1).

A 100-fold molar excess of unlabeled calcitriol displaced [$^3$H]$1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ from the 3.5 S peak, while a 100-fold excess of $25(\text{OH})\text{D}_3$ caused only a minor change. Competition was even less with $1(\text{OH})\text{D}_3$ and $24(\text{R}),25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$. This finding indicates that [$^3$H]$1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ binds specifically to a 3.5 S macromolecule.

To validate the technique used, chick intestine, i.e., a tissue with known $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ receptor content [20] was examined in parallel and showed virtually identical binding by a 3.5 S macromolecule.

At high ionic strength unoccupied nuclear receptors may be mobilized into the cytoplasmic fraction as previously demonstrated [21]. Indeed, in three separate experiments, binding of calcitriol in the cytosolic fraction was about twice as high when the epidermis had been homogenized in the presence of 0.4 M KCl as compared to 0.2 M KCl (Fig. 2). Figure 1A (lower panel) shows that at high ionic strength [$^3$H]$24(\text{R}),25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ and [$^3$H]$25(\text{OH})\text{D}_3$ binds to a 6 S macromolecule. This confirms that a separate binding protein is present in the cytosolic fraction of neonatal mouse epidermis, which is distinct from the calcitriol receptor and exhibits similar affinities for $24(\text{R}),25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ and $25(\text{OH})\text{D}_3$. Such cytosolic binding protein is also found in other tis-

sues [12, 22, 23] and is thought to correspond to a
binding protein derived from plasma.

Competition Studies with Other Vitamin D Metabolites in the Cytosol of Neonatal Mice Epidermis

The specificity of the $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ receptor was ex-amined by studying the relative binding affinities for other vitamin D metabolites using competition binding assay procedures. Cytosol from neonatal epidermis prepared in KTED buffer was incubated with 2 nM $[^3\text{H}]1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ and a variable molar excess of different unlabeled vitamin D metabolites for 16 h at $4^\circ\text{C}$. Specific binding was determined using the hydroxylapatite assay and substracting non-specific binding from total binding as described above. The amount of $[^3\text{H}]1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ bound spe-cifically in the absence of competing ligand is given as 100\% (see Fig. 5) and averaged 56 fmol/mg protein. Figure 5 shows the relative affinity of other vitamin D metabolites for the $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ receptor. Its numerical values ($\text{EC}_{50}$) correspond to the ab-solute concentrations of a given metabolite required to displace $[^3\text{H}]1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ by 50\%. Obviously unl-abeled $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ was the best competitor, one-fold molar excess reducing $[^3\text{H}]1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ binding by 50\%. To achieve a similar effect with $25(\text{OH})\text{D}_3$ or $1(\text{OH})\text{D}_3$, 80- and 200-fold molar ex-cess had to be employed.

When primary epidermal cell cultures were treated with $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ at different concentrations ($10^{-11}$ to $10^{-6}$ M) and incubated for 24, 48, 72, and 96 h, respectively, pulse labeling with $[^{3}\text{H}]$dThd for 1 h showed a dose-dependent inhibitory effect on DNA synthesis at concentrations exceeding $10^{-10}$ M. At $10^{-11}$ Mvalues were not significantly different from solvent controls. Figure 7 shows one representative experiment of four independent series. Each value in the graph represents the mean of six replicate incubations. DNA yield was similar in $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ and solvent treated preparations. $25(\text{OH})\text{D}_3$;$24,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$; and $1(\text{OH})\text{D}_3$ had no significant effects at physiological concentrations, but caused variable inhibitions at $10^{-6}$ M (data not given).
Discussion
The preceding results demonstrate the presence of $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ receptors in basal cells of the epi-
dermis of the neonatal and adult mouse and document decreased radiothymidine incorporation in primary mouse epidermal cell cultures under the influence of $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$.

The $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ receptor was found in the cytosol as well as in the nuclear fraction. With respect to its affinity, sedimentation characteristics, and chemical properties the binding macromolecule resembles $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ receptor proteins found in chick intestinal mucosa [20], pancreas [24], bone [25], parathyroid gland [26], pituitary [27, 28], mammary glands [29], placenta [30], testis [12], and various tumor cell lines [31-35].

The formal demonstration of a $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ receptor in non-cultured basal cells of the epidermis of the neonatal mouse further extends previous communications, which reported binding of $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ by cultured human keratinocytes and fibroblasts [4] and whole rat skin [36] as well as autoradiographic binding of $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ to rat epidermis, preferentially basal cells [37].

Sedimentation coefficients at high ionic strength [38] for all $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ receptors, including the one in epidermis, varied between 3.5 and 3.7 S, clearly distinct from 3.9 to 4.1 S serum binding proteins (data not given) and 6 S $25(\text{OH})\text{D}_3$ tissue binding
J. Merke et al.: 1,25-Dihydroxyvitamin D Receptors in Skin

protein. High binding specificity for $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ was established in epidermis by competition studies. Homogeneity of the binding macromolecule is also suggested by the results of Scatchard analysis, which reveals the presence of a single class of non-interacting binding sites in neonatal as well as adult epidermis.

Previous studies have shown binding of $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ in nuclear and cytosolic fractions of whole mouse skin $\textit{in vivo}$ and $\textit{in vitro}$ [39]. Further extending previous autoradiographic findings [37], our studies show localization of $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ receptors in the basal, i.e., the mitotically active, but not suprabasal cells of the epidermis. It is of note that $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ receptors are expressed in neonatal skin. The equilibrium dissociation constant $K_D$ is the same range as circulating $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ concentrations in rodents [41]. This suggests that occupancy of the receptor varies with hormone concentrations in the physiological range. The conclusion of partial receptor occupancy in vivo is also supported by the finding that $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ receptor recovery was twice as high in cytosol fractions prepared at high ionic strength (KTED) as compared to low ionic strength (TED). Previous observations of Walters et al. [21] demonstrated that 90\% of the unoccupied receptors for $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ remain in the nuclear fraction when chick intestinal mucosa is homogenized in low salt buffer, but appear in the cytosolic fraction when homogenates are prepared in high salt buffer, suggesting translocation of unoccupied nuclear receptors into the cytosol at high ionic strength.

Demonstration of epidermal $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ receptors is in agreement with recent findings of $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ receptors in organs other than classical calcium regulating tissues and raises the question of their biological function. Skin [1], and specifically epidermis [42], plays an important role in vitamin D metabolism since it is the site of prevtamin D3 photosynthesis. Chronic dosing with calcitriol caused a fourfold increase in skin 7-dehydrocholesterol content of vitamin D-deficient rats [43], suggesting positive feedback regulation of vitamin D production in skin by $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$. So far it is unknown, whether such regulation is mediated by receptor interaction.

Furthermore, it was shown that maximal induction by UV radiation of skin tyrosinase, a marker
of melanogenesis, requires cholecalciferol. In melanoma cell culture systems, cholecalciferol has also
been shown to stimulate melanogenesis [3]. No information is available on whether $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$, as
opposed to cholecalciferol, does influence melanogenesis and growth of normal and malignant melanocytes. It should be noted that contamination of

the basal epidermal cell fraction by melanocytes has not been formally excluded in the present study; this possibility appears remote, however, since mi- croscopical analysis showed that less than 3\% of the basal cell fraction were melanocytes in normal skin; in the present study an albino strain was used and melanocytes could not be quantitated.

Calcium binding protein is one gene product expressed under the influence of $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ in the cytosol of the basal layer of the epidermis [44], but its role in basal cell function has not been defined. Further potential actions of $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ concerned growth regulation. In receptor-positive normal fibroblasts, $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ causes a dose-dependent inhibition of cell growth [7]. The presence of cytosolic 1,25(OH)2D3 receptor in skin fibroblasts may be necessary for expression of a growth inhibitory effect of 1,25(OH)2D3 [4]. Such action of 1,25(OH)2D3 would be in line with previous studies in hematopoetic cells [45, 46]. In addition, 1,25(OH)2D3 has been shown to exert growth control in proliferating melanoma cells [35]. The hypothesis has been advanced that $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ induces cellular differentiation by mechanisms similar to classical steroid hormones. In view of these findings, the localization of $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ receptors in the proliferative compartment of epidermis is of interest, particularly in view of our demonstration of $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ receptor binding to DNA, reversible with 0.25 M KCl, which suggests genomic interaction. Our present experiments establish the time course of $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ action on basal epidermal cell proliferation. They confirm and extend measurements of Hosomi et al. [40] after 20 h of incubation and document dose-dependent inhibition, at least at $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ concentrations above $10^{-11}$ M. A slight increase at $10^{-11}$ M was not statistically significant in extended series of experiments.

Our assay system offers some perspectives. We feel that demonstration of $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ receptors in epidermal cells holds promise as an investigative tool. We [47] and others [48] were able to demonstrate calcitriol receptors in transformed, but not in normal circulatory lymphocytes. Although some $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ receptors are demonstrable on human monocytes [47], human blood cells may not be suited for studies on regulation of $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ receptors. Use of skin biopsies, i.e., a composite of several cell species, has been proposed by Feldman [7] and human skin fibroblasts and cultured keratin- ocytes have been examined in the syndrome of $1,25(\text{OH})_2\text{D}_3$ unresponsiveness [4, 5, 8, 49]. Use of uncultured human basal epidermal cell preparations would avoid both contamination with non-basal cells and phenotypic modulation of receptors during culture $\textit{in vitro}$. Induction of Endochondral Bone by Demineralized Bone Matrix from Diabetic Rats
Richard Landesman$^*$ and A. H. Reddi
Bone Cell Biology Section, Mineralized Tissue Research Branch, National Institute of Dental Research, National Institutes of Health,Bethesda,Maryland 20205

$\textbf{Summary:}$: In this investigation we examined the osteoinductive potential of demineralized bone matrix derived from chronically diabetic (streptozotocin-induced) rats. Long-Evans rats (28-31 days) were made diabetic with a single injection of streptozotocin (65 mg/kg) and provided food and water $\textit{ad lib}$ for 2 months. Diaphyseal shafts of femurs and tibias removed from the diabetic rats and their sibling controls were dehydrated, pulverized, sieved to 74-420 $\mu$m particles, and demineralized. Matrix was then bioassayed for its ability to induce endochondral bone on day 11 following subcutaneous implantation over the thorax of Long-Evans rats. The resulting plaques of tissue were subjected to histological analysis, determination of alkaline phosphatase activity, and calcium content. Bone matrix derived from diabetic animals proved to be a significantly better inducer of endochondral bone than did control matrix.
$\textbf{Key words}$: Endochondral bone formation — Osteoinductive potential - Diabetic bone matrix — Streptozotocin-induced diabetes.

Subcutaneous implantation of allogenec demineralized diaphyseal bone matrix results in the sequential development of cartilage and bone in the rat [1- 3]. Following a brief inflammatory response (day 1) fibroblastlike mesenchymal cells invade the area of the implant and proliferate by day 3. This stage is followed by a period of chondrogenesis (days 5-7), calcification of the cartilage matrix (days 9--12), and

ossification and marrow development (days 14-20) [4]. The early stages of the induction and endochondral bone formation in the streptozotocin-induced diabetic rat, following the implantation of demineralized bone matrix from normal rats, are decreased and delayed through day 9 as a consequence of impaired mesenchymal cell proliferation and reduced mineralization [5]. This inhibition was fully corrected by daily insulin injections. Normal long bone development and matrix formation are diminished in the rat following streptozotocin treatment both acutely (5-10 days posttreatment) as well as in the chronically diabetic animal (7 weeks) [6,7].

Considering the fact that diabetic rat bones are in a low state of turnover and reduced in their number of osteocytes and matrix components compared with controls or insulin-treated animals [6, 7] we were interested in determining the osteoinductive potential of bone matrix from chronically diabetic rats. Are changes in the bone matrix in diabetes partially responsible for poor fracture healing?
Materials and Methods
Diabetic Animals

Forty male rats (Long-Evans strain, 28-31 days) weighing between 100-120 g were made diabetic by a single intravenous injection of streptozotocin (65 mg/kg) suspended in 0.01 M citrate buffer at pH 4.5 [9, 10]. The experimental rats and their sibling controls were provided food and water ad lib for 2 months.
